extracted.intended_audience: academics and researchers invited to peer review book proposals for publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for academics/researchers on how to conduct effective peer reviews of book proposals (and sample chapters/manuscripts) for publishing houses, including process, evaluation criteria, recommended structure of reviews, and recommendation categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can take a range of forms: single-blind, double-blind, open peer review, and post-publication peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-blind: author does not know reviewer identity but reviewers know author (the vast majority of book reviews). Double-blind: neither authors nor reviewers know one another. Open: identities known to one another. Post-publication: manuscripts reviewed after publication; reviews often open and published alongside the article. Advantages and disadvantages generally stem from attitudes to openness versus anonymity (openness increases visibility; anonymity can protect reviewers and allow more candid evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review editorial checks and materials provided
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical steps that usually take place before you are asked to review a book: commissioning editor may have discussed the idea with the author; author submits a proposal (sometimes sample chapters or full manuscript); editor performs an initial check to ensure necessary information is present; editor may ask for additional information; editor and author may amend proposal prior to peer review; editor decides whether to send to peer review and finds appropriate reviewers; invitation is then sent to reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that proposals you receive may have been through prior editorial discussion and initial screening; editors may supply supplementary materials (sample chapters, table of contents) and/or specific questions for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding whether to accept the invitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether you have the appropriate expertise, whether you have any conflict of interest, and whether you have the time to complete the review by the requested deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not confident in your ability to assess the whole proposal, discuss with the editor about commenting on specific aspects or declining. Declare any potential conflicts of interest to the editor. If unable to meet the deadline, notify the editor promptly; if declining, respond quickly and, where possible, suggest alternative reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow editor requests and guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Read any peer review guidelines and specific questions the editor provides when you accept an invitation to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors might suggest key considerations and a recommended review structure—read these carefully and adapt your review to meet the editor’s requirements. If unsure about particular requirements, ask the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: First reading — overview of proposal and contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: On first reading form an overall impression and understanding of the book proposal and any supplementary information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make notes on first impressions, focusing on recent related work in the area, responding to the book’s statement of purpose, and thinking about the impact the book might have on the general body of research in the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second reading — contribution to the discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the book makes a significant contribution to the discipline and whether there is a need for a book on the subject at the proposed level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to consider: Does this book make a significant contribution at this time? Is there a need at the proposed level? Is there a clear readership and has the author explained the target audience? Has the author situated the book among competitors and explained how it differs? Are there major competitors (published or in preparation) not mentioned? Would you use this book for a class or recommend to students? Is the subject area expanding, static or contracting? Is the useful life of the book likely to be 3, 5 or 10 years?

rubrics_metrics.name: Second reading — academic rigour and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the scholarly soundness and accuracy of the proposed methodology, argument, and supporting information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the methodology or argument is academically sound and/or convincing and original; whether appropriate related topics and research literature are mentioned; whether there are obvious gaps in coverage; whether information (data, formulae, quotations, references, tables and figures) in the proposal and sample chapters is accurate and correct; and whether you are familiar with the author(s)’ work and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second reading — style, structure and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the proposed structure, organisation, coverage relative to proposed length, and clarity of language in the proposal and any sample chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Is the proposed structure (and table of contents where available) clear and well-organised? Is there extraneous material that could be omitted? Can the material be covered in the proposed length? Is the language in the proposal and sample chapters clear and accurate? Make notes related to each area and substantiate evaluations with examples from the proposal or sample chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for different kinds of book (textbooks and series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that textbooks and books proposed for series may require different or additional considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks: editors will often ask more detailed questions about proposed audience, level and pedagogical features and may provide additional guidance. Series: if the book is proposed for an existing series, be asked to comment on its suitability for that series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and content of the review
rubrics_metrics.description: Organise your written review so it summarises your overall judgement and then substantiates that judgement with detailed evidence and suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many reviewers summarise their thoughts in the first paragraphs, then in the second half move onto detailed substantiation of recommendations with suggestions for revisions where needed. Substantiate evaluations with examples from the proposal and/or sample chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation categories and what they imply
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear recommendation to the editor: Accept without revision; Accept with revisions; or Do not accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept without revision: rare. Accept with revisions: most accepted books require amendments—possible revisions include broadening or narrowing coverage, including additional topics or references, aiming at a more appropriate audience, building on certain areas (e.g., significance, competitors), and addressing language problems and measures to deal with them. Do not accept: if the proposal is unsound in principle or methodology, or does not make a significant contribution—give objective reasons and evidence so the editor understands your concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting the review — deadlines and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit your review to the editor by the agreed deadline, ensuring it accurately reflects your professional opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor will read and consider your review, collate reviewers’ recommendations (usually anonymising them), and send feedback to the author or general feedback based on the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional review rounds and clearance reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: You may be asked to review revised proposals or perform a clearance review to check that previous comments have been addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asked to review again, compare your initial review against the revised material to ensure proposed changes were made successfully; suggest additional changes if needed. A clearance review checks that initial comments were sufficiently addressed and allows you to comment on other areas (e.g., how well the manuscript achieves proposed aims). Most books have one or two revision stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: After the review — editorial decision and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Final decision is taken by the editor, and if accepted a contract will be drawn up; reviewers may receive a copy of the published book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that your role is advisory — the editor collates final comments and makes the decision. If the book is accepted you may be sent a copy upon publication.
